contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: Der Kobra-Effekt in der KI-Transformation: So misst du den Erfolg deiner KI-Strategie, ohne den Fehler zu wiederholen, an dem schon Agile-Transformationen gescheitert sind
items.summary: Seit Jahresbeginn begleite ich ein Unternehmen bei der Einführung von KI. Wie du dir denken kannst, dreht sich ein großer Teil meiner Arbeit um eine Frage: Woran lässt sich der Erfolg der KI-Transformationen festmachen? Die Antworten ließen mich aufhorchen: „Jeder Mitarbeiter nutzt in der täglichen Arbeit KI.“ „KI-Tools liefern 95 % Genauigkeit bei allen Ergebnissen.“ „Die Tokennutzung in der Entwicklung steigt um 25 %.“ Moment mal, diese Sätze kenne ich doch schon: „Alle Teams arbeiten nach Scrum.“ „95 % der geplanten User-Stories wurden umgesetzt.“ „Entwicklerteams liefern 25 % mehr Velocity.“ Erst Scrum, dann SAFe, nun KI. Wiederholt sich die Geschichte der Transformationen – und wiederholen sich mit ihr die Fehler? Dieser Frage gehen wir heute nach. Los geht’s ... Über 80 % der Entwickler sollten KI wöchentlich einsetzen. Diese Vorgabe war Teil einer Initiative bei Amazon. Dazu sollten über 2100 Entwicklerteams angehalten werden, KI in ihre Arbeitsweise zu integrieren. Die Erwartungen seitens Amazon waren hoch: Die Führung von Amazon erhoffte sich, dass die meisten Teams ihre Software-Release-Geschwindigkeit verdreifachen würden, eine kleinere Gruppe von mindestens 25 Teams sogar eine Verzehnfachung des Outputs erreichen würde. Erfolgsdruck führte dazu, dass 30000 Stellen gestrichen wurden und rund 200 Milliarden Dollar investiert wurden, vor allem in KI- und Rechenzentrumsinfrastruktur. Ab November 2025 priorisierte Amazon deshalb die Nutzung des Entwicklungswerkzeugs Kiro. In einem internen Memo, das Reuters einsehen konnte , hieß es, man mache Kiro zum „empfohlenen KI-nativen Entwicklungstool für Amazon“. Das Memo wurde unter anderem von Dave Treadwell, Senior Vice President bei Amazon, unterzeichnet. Kiro ist ein eigener agentischer Coding-Assistent, der aus Prompts Spezifikationen, Code, Dokumentation und Tests erzeugt. Um zu zeigen, wie sehr KI die Arbeit beschleunigen kann, erstellte im Frühjahr 2026 eine Gruppe von Mitarbeitern ein informelles Leaderboard namens KiroRank. KiroRank machte die KI-Aktivität einzelner Entwickler anhand des Token-Verbrauchs sichtbar: Wer vorne lag, bekam Awards, kleine Abzeichen, die neben dem Namen erschienen. Ein anonymer Amazon-Entwickler beschrieb die Auswirkung davon so: Der Druck, diese Tools zu nutzen, sei enorm. Manche Kollegen setzten Agenten ausschließlich ein, um ihren Token-Verbrauch zu maximieren. Und obwohl Amazon den Mitarbeitenden offenbar mitgeteilt hatte, dass ihre KI-Nutzungsstatistiken nicht in Leistungsbeurteilungen einfließen würden, glaubten das nicht alle Beschäftigten. „Manager schauen darauf“, sagte ein weiterer Mitarbeiter. Das Ergebnis war keine Wertschöpfung mehr, sondern ein Anstieg der Kosten. Gartner prognostiziert e vor Kurzem, dass die KI-Coding-Kosten pro Entwickler bis zum Jahr 2028 dessen durchschnittliches Gehalt übersteigen werden. Im Mai zog Dave Treadwell die Reißleine und richtete sich an die Mitarbeiter von Amazon: „Bitte setzt KI nicht nur ein, um KI einzusetzen. Nutzt KI, um Kundenprobleme zu lösen, Geschäftsprobleme zu lösen und Innovation voranzutreiben.“ Die Geschichte von Amazon ist dabei nur ein Beispiel. Es wiederholt sich bei vielen Transformationen: Anfang des 20. Jahrhunderts, so erzählt man es sich, setzte die britische Kolonialverwaltung in Delhi ein Kopfgeld auf tote Kobras aus, um die Schlangenplage einzudämmen. Findige Inder taten das Naheliegende: Sie züchteten Kobras, um sie gegen Prämie abzuliefern. Als die Behörde das Programm einstellte, ließen die Züchter ihre nun wertlosen Tiere frei. Am Ende gab es mehr Schlangen als zuvor. Seither trägt das Phänomen einen Namen: der Kobra-Effekt. Wenn ein gut gemeinter Anreiz genau das Gegenteil dessen bewirkt, was er bezwecken sollte. KiroRank lässt sich auch mit diesem Effekt beschreiben. Der Ökonom Goodhart formulierte es so: Sobald eine Kennzahl zum Ziel wird, taugt sie nicht mehr als Kennzahl. KiroRank ist gerade deshalb so lehrreich, weil es eine sehr typische Falle bei Transformationen ist. Nur eben in einer neuen technologischen Verpackung. Früher war es Scrum, dann SAFe und jetzt KI. Am Ende folgt sie ähnlichen Mustern: Wenn ein Unternehmen Anpassungen über sichtbare Aktivität belohnt (mehr Story-Points, mehr Scrum-Teams, mehr Scrum-Meetings), dann bekommt es in der Regel genau das. Menschen sind nicht irrational, sie optimieren auf das, was sichtbar zählt. KiroRank wurde am 29. Mai abgeschaltet. Ein Amazon-Sprecher distanzierte sich offiziell davon und ordnete es im Nachgang als informellen, von einer Gruppe von Mitarbeitenden gebauten Tracker ein. Er „war nie dazu gedacht, die Nutzung von KI um der Nutzung willen zu fördern.“ Man habe damit lediglich zeigen wollen, wie KI Arbeit beschleunigen kann. Laut der Financial Times richtete Amazon seither den Blick stärker auf „normalised deployments“. Also auf die Frage, ob die KI tatsächlich Code in Produktion bringt. „Code in Produktion“ ist eine bessere Kennzahl als der Token-Verbrauch. Aber ... ...…

items.title: Your framework isn't broken. Your fundamentals are.
items.summary: Image You've done the reorganization. You've swapped the framework, maybe more than once. Scrum, then a bit of SAFe, then something homegrown. New ceremonies, a new tool. And the same problems came back. The status that was green until it snapped. The retro that produces conversation and no change. The decision that got made properly in the meeting and then unmade in the hallway. The team that waits more than it works. The release nobody checks on. If you've been reading along these past weeks, you've met all five. And here's the thing they have in common: not one of them was caused by the framework. You can run any of them by the book and still hit every one. That should be a relief, actually. It means the expensive thing you keep reaching for, the next framework, the next transformation, was never going to fix it. Because it was never the framework. What's actually underneath Every way of working, Scrum or SAFe or Kanban or your own hybrid, sits on top of a set of behaviors. When the behaviors are there, the framework looks like it's working. When they're missing, the same framework looks broken. Same ceremonies, same board, completely different results, and the difference isn't the process. It's whether the team actually does the things the process assumes. That's the whole idea we build on: behavior creates professionalism, not frameworks. A framework is a container. What you put in it is the fundamentals. There are eight of them. Every friction you've felt traces back to one being weak. The eight fundamentals Three of them form a loop, the engine that lets a team learn: Reality Transparency. The real state of the work, its progress, quality, and risk, is visible and understood the same way by everyone. Honest Inspection. The team looks at that real state without flinching, and names the problems truthfully instead of reporting the comfortable version. Decisive Adaptation. When the team learns something, it changes what it does, while the change is still cheap. Three hold up how the team works together: Trust and Candor. It's safe to tell each other the truth, including the inconvenient truth, without it costing you. Outcome Ownership. The team treats the result of its work as its business, someone goes back and looks at whether it worked. Decision Mandate. The team has the authority to make the decisions its work actually requires. And two decide whether the team can deliver at all: Skill Completeness. The team has enough of the skills it needs to move without a handoff for every step. Commitment to Quality. The team holds a real, non-negotiable standard for "done." Read back over your last quarter and the frictions sort themselves. The green status that snapped was Reality Transparency and Honest Inspection. The hallway meeting was Trust and Candor. The team that waits was Skill Completeness. Each visible problem, what we call a Friction Signal, points to a specific fundamental underneath it that's weak. Why this changes what you do next If the problem were the framework, the fix would be a new framework, and you've run that experiment. If the problem is a weak fundamental, the fix is smaller and more precise: find the one that's actually under pressure, and change one behavior, then watch what shifts. That's what the Fundamentals First Repair System is: a way to trace the friction your team feels to the fundamental that's causing it, and repair it directly. It doesn't install on top of your framework the way each transformation did. Over the coming weeks, we take the eight one at a time: what each one really is, how you know it's weak, and a small move that could help rebuild it. Starting with the one most teams are missing first. For now, the fastest way in is to find out which fundamental is under the most pressure on your own team. It takes about two minutes. Take the two-minute self-diagnostic Your framework isn't broken. Your fundamentals are. Scrum on!

items.title: The Role of Agency in Scrum: Why Self-Management Without Agency is a Lie
items.summary: Originally published on Engineering Leadership . Scrum is often misunderstood as a set of ceremonies or a lightweight project management method. It is neither. Scrum is a social technology built around the ethos of Agile, enabling teams to deliver adaptive solutions in complex environments. At its core lies a fundamental, non-negotiable requirement: self-management. But self-management is not simply a label you apply to teams. It demands something deeper and harder: real agency. Without agency, Scrum collapses into shallow ritual. Without agency, accountability is performative, not real. Without agency, you are not doing Scrum. You are enacting a fragile imitation of agility. Scrum Is Agile , and Agile Demands Self-Management Agile and Scrum are often conflated or treated as separate. Let us be clear: True Scrum is Agile. Scrum operationalises Agile principles with discipline, transparency, and empiricism. It creates a bounded environment where teams can thrive. The Agile Manifesto (2001) made it clear: The best architectures, requirements, and designs emerge from self-organizing teams. Self-organisation was never about anarchy. It was about teams owning how they deliver value . Agile assumes teams will figure out the best way to achieve goals , not be told exactly what to do. Scrum sharpened this requirement in the 2020 Scrum Guide: Scrum Teams are cross-functional and self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and how. Self-management is not a bonus feature. It is the foundation. Without it, Scrum is impossible. Agency: The Prerequisite for Accountability Agency is the power to make decisions and act toward outcomes you are accountable for. It is inseparable from accountability itself. Without agency, accountability is a façade , a mechanism for assigning blame rather than empowering success. Scrum defines clear accountabilities: Product Owner : Maximising value. Developers : Delivering a usable Increment every Sprint. Scrum Master : Enabling the Scrum Team’s effectiveness. These accountabilities assume that those who hold them have real authority to act . When organisations strip away decision-making power but leave accountability in place, they are not enabling agility. They are constructing a system of learned helplessness. The Myth of “Self-Managing” Teams Many organisations today claim to embrace “self-managing teams” but operate in ways that directly undermine them: Sprint Goals are dictated, not created. Work is assigned to individuals by managers. Technical decisions are second-guessed by external authorities. This is not self-management. This is hierarchical command-and-control wrapped in daily standups and sticky notes. If your team cannot decide how to achieve the Sprint Goal, they are not self-managing. They are being managed under a different name. Weak Scrum Masters Enable Weak Scrum Scrum Masters are accountable for the effectiveness of the Scrum Team . Yet in practice, many are limited to scheduling events and taking notes , with no real authority to challenge systemic dysfunction. A Scrum Master without agency is not fulfilling their accountability. They are facilitating ceremony without enabling change. Scrum Masters must: Teach leadership and teams what true self-management entails. Coach teams to take ownership of their processes and outcomes. Mentor individuals to step into accountability with courage. Facilitate organisational evolution, not just event logistics. If you are a Scrum Master and you cannot do these things because of organisational resistance , you must raise it visibly. Otherwise, you are complicit in the degradation of Scrum. Why Weak Implementations Collapse When organisations adopt the appearance of Scrum without enabling the conditions for Scrum, dysfunction inevitably follows: Daily Scrums become status reporting. Sprint Reviews become formalities with no real inspection. Retrospectives become meaningless because the team lacks the power to change anything. Scrum without agency becomes a theatre production. A ritualistic reenactment of agility, without any of the outcomes. When organisations complain that “ Scrum doesn’t work ,” the reality is usually simpler: they refused to enable it to work , and they ignore the evidence of their own dysfunction. The Path Forward: Fight for Agency If you are serious about creating real, resilient agility: Scrum Masters must coach, teach, mentor, and cause real change , not just facilitate ceremonies. Product Owners must demand the authority to own the backlog and drive product strategy. Developers must guard their right to decide how to build and deliver working product Increments. And leadership must understand: if you want the results Scrum promises, you must create the environment Scrum requires. Self-management is not optional. Agency is not optional. items.title: Scrum Day India 2026 Recap: Scrum Teams in the Age of Autonomous Agents
items.summary: Image On Saturday, 26 September 2026, Scrum practitioners gathered at To The New in Sector 144, Noida, for Scrum Day India 2026. The theme was Scrum Teams in the Age of Autonomous Agents . For the last two years, most conversations about AI in Scrum have been about assistance: a better first draft of a user story, a faster summary of a Sprint Review. This year's sessions started from a different place. Agents now pick up Product Backlog items, run checks, and produce Increments alongside the humans on the team. So the question was not whether Scrum still works. It was what Scrum Masters, Product Owners, and Developers have to do differently when part of the work is done by something that cannot be accountable. Seven practitioners answered that question across six sessions. Recordings and slides are going up session by session on the Scrum Day India 2026 session hub . Below is what each session covered, the threads that ran through all of them, and a few questions worth taking into your next Sprint Retrospective. The six sessions When AI Joins the Sprint: What Should Humans Stop Doing, Start Doing, and Never Delegate? Jaspreet Singh Chawla, Senior Business Analyst, To The New Jaspreet walked through what AI can now carry in each part of the work. In discovery it reads specification documents and Jira history to expose hidden dependencies and draft acceptance criteria. In refinement it flags ambiguous constraints and estimation risks. In development and testing it generates code iterations and builds test suites from past defect patterns. His answer to "so what do humans do?" is a five-part discipline for every AI-assisted workflow: See what the AI has already analyzed, Do only the work that needs judgment, Challenge outputs that look overconfident or incomplete, Stop manual work the AI handles reliably, and Own the final decision. The last one is non-delegable. Watch Jaspreet's session The Scrum Master's New Teammate: Autonomous AI Agents Shalini Khanna, Scrum Master, Coforge Shalini's opening line set the tone: AI is not taking Scrum Master jobs, it is removing the administrative comfort zone. Much of the tracking and documentation that filled a Scrum Master's week can now be handled by agents. What remains is the harder part of the accountability: coaching, risk mitigation, and improving flow. She showed two agents her teams use. An AI Release Coordinator connects to Azure DevOps and produces standardized, business-friendly release notes across teams. An AI Knowledge Partner pulls scattered knowledge from design documents, release notes, and user stories into one place. In her experience, it cut onboarding from weeks to days. Watch Shalini's session The AI-Native Software Team: From Personal AI to Autonomous Delivery Chetan Arora, Global Director – Enterprise Transformation & AI Strategy, Nagarro Chetan opened with a productivity paradox. He cited industry figures showing that most organizations use AI and most developers report personal productivity gains. Yet only a small minority see a financial payback within a year, or better team collaboration. His explanation: individual speed does not become business impact until the delivery system itself changes. He described three levels, AI for Me, AI for Engineering, and AI for Delivery. When code generation gets faster, the bottleneck moves upstream to discovery and planning, and downstream to testing and release. His model sorts work on a scale from human judgment to AI autonomy. Humans keep vision, strategy, trade-offs, and accountability. AI augments analysis. Agents take bounded tasks with explicit guardrails. Rule-based routine work is automated. Watch Chetan's session KPI Blueprint for Agentic AI Workflows Deepti Jain, Agentic Workflow Specialist Deepti made the case that chatbot metrics fail for agents. A chatbot is judged one response at a time. An agent plans, calls tools, and executes multi-step work, where one error can break a workflow or change data. She proposed KPIs in three tiers: operational (autonomous completion rate, human escalation rate, cycle time), technical and financial (tool accuracy, LLM cost per completed task), and business impact (net human hours saved and a "Trust Curve" for how much oversight an agent still needs). Her cost section was the most practical of the day. Agentic loops often run 5 to 15 internal turns, and each turn resends the growing history, so a single query can consume tens of thousands of tokens. Her fix is model cascading: a premium model plans and reviews, smaller models handle sub-tasks. In her example, cost per task fell by more than half at the same accuracy. Watch Deepti's session When Half of Your Team Is AI Agents Sanjay Saini, Professional Scrum Trainer and Founder, AgileWoW My own session looked at the Scrum framework itself. items.title: 5 Things the Scrum Master Shouldn’t Be Doing
items.summary: Image I love being a Scrum Master. What I love about it is helping a team accomplish something and honestly just making Developers' work lives as hassle-free as possible. I love working with smart people and seeing them accomplish amazing things. As a Scrum Master, most of us want to help. But sometimes we think we are helping when we’re actually hurting the team. As a case in point, when I was a new Scrum Master, I was looking for how to add value to the team. So, I observed that submitting security and access requests was an annoying administrative job for the Developers. I suggested that I could help take those over for Developers. What began as a way to help quickly became a bottleneck. Pretty soon one of the Developers asked me, in an annoyed tone, if they had to submit these through me because it would be faster just to do it themselves. It was a lesson I haven’t forgotten. Sometimes helpfulness can be annoying. Sometimes knowing what NOT to do can be as helpful as knowing what TO do. Here are five things that the Scrum Master shouldn’t be doing. 1) Gatekeeper No, I’m not talking about security access again. I once worked at an organization where instead of being the Scrum Master I was a stakeholder. I needed to request work from the Scrum team, and I knew it was a quick five-minute job, so I emailed my request to the Product Owner. Instead of adding the request to the Product Backlog (or telling me “no”), I got a snippy email from the Scrum Master a week later telling me that all requests for the Scrum team had to go through her. I decided to play by her rules and sent her a reply with my request, explaining that it was urgently needed. Ten back-and-forth emails and a couple of unanswered calls later, I finally actually gave up. Some months later I received an email from a Developer asking for details about my request. I was surprised because I didn't know my work request had even been added to the Product Backlog, so by that time the business had developed a work-around. What I remember about this request was not so much the request itself but the frustration and lack of visibility around working with that Scrum team. 2) Organizing the Scrum Team into teams I observed a Scrum Master once who was working to roll out Scrum to a new area of the business. One of the managers (who didn’t work directly with that team) met with other executives (who also didn’t work directly with those team members) and they put a lot of thought into how the teams should be structured and who should be on each team. It was well intended and well thought-out, but totally unnecessary. A better approach would have been to let the team self-organize. On the many occasions where I have let teams self-organize, they mostly don’t come up with anything different or better or worse than what executives would have come up with. (Well, to be honest, usually it’s a bit better than what the executives would have come up with.) But the important thing is that they make it work because it was their own idea. And that makes all the difference. I did this once with a team of sixty people remotely. They came up with their team structure, and they were empowered to decide who would be on each team. It improved morale. It made them feel in control of their own work. And it made them more collaborative than they otherwise would have been. Six months later, when priorities changed, they decided one day at a Retrospective that they needed to re-organize to meet the new business needs. And so they did. No management intervention needed. 3) Making decisions for the Scrum Team If your team is facing a larger decision, it isn’t up to the Scrum Master to navigate this for them. What the Scrum Master can do is bring together the team members for a discussion and let them decide how to accomplish it. For example, if the team is doing some greenfield development and they need to make a major architectural decision, I have often had Developers ask me to schedule a meeting to bring the right people together to discuss it. I facilitate the meeting in such a way as to make it productive. That’s my part as the Scrum Master. But I don’t make the decision for them. If they need to request approvals from higher-ups due to it being a significant decision, I ask how they want to go about that. Usually, it’s a follow-up meeting with leadership. 4) Owning the Sprint Review Now this one is a bit nuanced. As the Scrum Master, it is my job to ensure that the Scrum events are positive, productive, and kept within the timebox. But the Sprint Review is the Product Owner’s most valuable event. items.title: Outcome-Based Leadership in Project Management: Measuring What Really Matters
items.summary: Image The Context I once led a software development program with more than 100 developers and several project managers. The projects were strategically important for the company, and expectations from upper leadership were high. Officially, the organization was working with Scrum. In practice, however, the organization was following a waterfall approach. Upper leadership was not satisfied with the program's performance. Project managers were also under increasing pressure to improve their individual performance. My mission was clear: get the program back on track and help the project managers reach a higher level of performance. But one question quickly became apparent: What exactly does good project management performance mean? The Problem: Measuring the Wrong Thing When asked how project manager performance was measured, top management struggled to provide a clear response. The answer usually came back to familiar project success metrics: On time. In budget. In scope. These metrics can be useful in managing project success (while usually falling short of adequately measuring project success). But they are not sufficient to evaluate project management performance. A project can miss a deadline because of changing customer requirements, technical challenges, organizational dependencies, or decisions made far outside the project manager's area of influence. Conversely, a project can remain on schedule and within budget while communication is poor, risks are hidden, and stakeholders are constantly surprised by what happens next. Project success and project management performance are related, but they are not the same thing. That raised a more fundamental question: If project managers should be led based on the outcomes produced, what is the actual outcome of project management? It obviously cannot be project success alone. Finding the Real Outcome I started looking for the answer by talking to the people involved. Stakeholders and project managers were asked a simple question: “How do you know that project managers are performing well and delivering great outcomes?” The “Five Whys” technique helped dig deeper: Whenever an answer described an activity, result, or indicator, the question was asked again in a slightly different form. The answers gradually moved away from project management activities and toward the actual experience of stakeholders. The surprising result was not to “keep the projects on schedule.” The more meaningful outcome was to “keep the number of unpleasant surprises down.” That was a breakthrough. Measuring Unpleasant Surprises In this particular context, reducing unpleasant surprises turned out to be a surprisingly powerful measure of project management effectiveness. Stakeholders became frustrated and pressure increased whenever unexpected information arrived unanticipated. The problem was not necessarily a changed timeline as such. For example, a stakeholder asking for an additional feature might make a milestone move. For them, this scenario did not automatically indicate poor project management. However, a last-minute confession that the team had already known for six weeks that the milestone would have to move posed a huge issue for these stakeholders. The difference is enormous. A changed timeline revealed at the last possible moment creates a surprise, destroys trust, and leaves little room for meaningful action. With this insight being clear, the program started measuring the number of unpleasant surprises per week. The measure was deliberately simple. Whenever I as the program manager was surprised by information that could reasonably have been known or communicated earlier, the situation was captured and discussed. The goal was to identify possible transparency and communication improvements. This changed the focus of project management. Instead of primarily asking: “Are we still on schedule?” the conversation increasingly leaned towards: “Does everyone who needs to know have the information needed to make good decisions?” From Measurement to Better Leadership The new focus created a much more useful basis for leading the project managers. Fewer unpleasant surprises meant better transparency, leading to earlier inspection and more opportunities for adaptation. Earlier adaptation increased the chances of achieving successful project outcomes. Schedule, budget, scope, quality, and other project metrics remained important. The difference was that these metrics were no longer treated as a direct proxy for project manager performance. Instead, the project management outcome became more closely connected to creating transparency and predictability for the people who depend on the project . The Takeaway Identifying the right outcome is not always easy. Especially in complex environments, it can be tempting to use easily measurable project metrics as a substitute for understanding the actual contribution of project management. items.title: Not All Complexity Can Be Processed Away. Fred Brooks Proved This in 1986.
items.summary: Image Every struggling product organization I sit with arrives at the same prescription: add more process, a pre-sprint refinement session, a mid-sprint review, more documents, more sign-offs, better status visibility. I have watched this pattern since 2010, and it almost never works. Most of what those organizations are dealing with cannot be fixed that way. The distinction was drawn by Fred Brooks in 1986, in a paper called "No Silver Bullet," delivered at the IFIP Tenth World Computing Conference. Brooks borrowed the framing from Aristotle, who separated essence from accident. Accidental difficulties "attend production but are not inherent" in the work. Essential difficulties are "inherent in the nature of the software." The first kind can be removed by better tooling, better languages, better process. The second is just what the work is. What Accidental Complexity Looks Like Brooks spent much of the paper locating past productivity gains in the accidental category. High-level languages removed the difficulty of mapping abstract intent onto machine instructions, delivering roughly a factor-of-five gain. Each gain was real but limited to removing what Brooks called "artificial barriers." Product work has its own supply of accidental complexity: backlogs with 300 items nobody navigates, release processes needing a week of setup per deployment. Another form is the steering committee sign-off that holds up development on work the team already understands. Better tooling, a trimmed backlog, tighter meetings reduce friction without changing the core work. Most product organizations know how to find gains in this category. The trouble is that fixing accidental complexity is real progress. That makes it easy to reach for when the actual problem is essential complexity. The Four Essential Difficulties Essential complexity cannot be removed without changing the problem. Brooks named four properties of software that resist simplification, and all four appear in product development. Complexity is the first essential difficulty Brooks named. Software entities are "more complex for their size than perhaps any other human construct, because no two parts are alike," and every scaling adds new kinds of elements, not just more of the same. Every product is a different answer to a different problem in a different context. Conformity is the second essential difficulty Brooks identified. Software must conform to interfaces it did not design; Brooks called this complexity "forced without rhyme or reason by the many human institutions and systems to which its interfaces must conform." For a product team this is the legacy infrastructure that limits what is deliverable. It is the legal requirement that arrives mid-Sprint, or the enterprise contract that specifies the API shape before the product is built. None of it simplifies out from the product side. The third essential difficulty, changeability, follows from success. Brooks described software as "pure thought-stuff, infinitely malleable," which means every successful product faces constant pressure to change as users invent new uses and markets shift. The pressure does not ease when planning becomes more detailed. Brooks named the fourth essential difficulty invisibility. A building has a floor plan; a circuit has a schematic. Software "has no ready geometric representation," and neither does the product problem it is meant to solve. Assumptions stay hidden until a Sprint Review proves them wrong, and dependencies only surface when they break. No process makes hidden things visible; it can only help them surface faster. A Counterargument The easy objection is that Brooks was writing about 1986-era software projects, not modern product management. That objection is fair on the specifics. False on the structure. All four essential properties appear in product work, because product work is also building abstract constructs in changing contexts. The properties follow from that, not from the decade. Why This Explains the Protocol and the Agenda I wrote recently about Scrum's two layers: a prescriptive, auditable protocol and an agenda that sets outcomes without specifying steps [3]. Brooks' framework shows what each layer is doing. The protocol does two things, and most teams only notice one. It reduces accidental complexity by governing choices that do not need judgment: fixing the Sprint length, respecting the timeboxes, defining the artifacts. And it builds structure that forces teams to confront essential complexity. The Sprint boundary limits how far changeability can compound before you inspect. The Sprint Review surfaces invisibility: hidden assumptions have to survive real use before the next Sprint. The protocol does not resolve the four essential difficulties. It makes them visible on a short enough schedule to respond. The agenda is discovering what users need and delivering it. That is where essential complexity has to be faced. You cannot specify value in advance;…

items.title: Does Your Organisation Need an AI Product Owner?
items.summary: Appointing one person accountable for AI is a sound first step. In an organisation moving to a product operating model, or already running one, the same role puts a dependency and a handoff between product teams and the decisions the model gives them. Most organisations adopted AI before anyone was accountable. Pilots started in several teams at once, and whichever area needed them first bought the licences. When an AI output went wrong, nobody could say who was accountable. In a 2026 BCG survey, half of respondents said their companies lacked clear governance for teams of people and AI, and almost as many named AI accountability among their three top concerns (Martin et al., 2026). Appointing an AI Product Owner gives the organisation one person who can make AI decisions, while ISO/IEC 42001 sets the same expectation: top management must ensure that responsibilities and authorities for the roles in an AI management system are assigned and communicated (International Organisation for Standardisation [ISO], 2023). As a first step, the role works. Executives know whom to ask about AI, and one person collects lessons from separate pilots instead of losing them when each pilot ends. The difficulty starts when the first step becomes the permanent design. Once an organisation commits to a product operating model, in which persistent product teams are accountable for outcomes (Cagan et al., 2024), an AI Product Owner holds the decisions the model assigns to each product's Product Owner, and every team that adopts AI adds to that one person's queue. Capable organisations create the role for a structural reason. When a new technology is adopted, the familiar response is to set up a function for it and appoint someone to run that function, because a project-funded organisation has no persistent product that could own the technology. The AI Product Owner is that response with a Scrum title. Manufacturers took the same path with quality: inspection departments checked work after it was done, until Deming (1986) argued that quality had to be built into the production process rather than inspected afterwards. AI is rarely a product The Scrum Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for maximising the value of the product that results from the Scrum Team's work. The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management: developing the Product Goal, creating and ordering Product Backlog items, and keeping the Product Backlog transparent (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). The Scrum Guide describes a product as a vehicle to deliver value, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers. Its Product Owner is "one person, not a committee", and succeeds only when the whole organisation respects their decisions. AI fails that definition in most organisations. It sits inside many products and has no boundary of its own; its stakeholders are everyone, and its users are teams already building other products. An AI Product Owner therefore holds no product in the Scrum Guide's sense, only an interest in how every other product is built. That interest conflicts with the Product Owners who already exist. Consider a team building a claims service, whose Product Owner is accountable for the value that service produces. If an AI Product Owner also decides how the team uses AI, what it prioritises or what it may release, the team answers to two people. When their decisions disagree, the organisation cannot respect both, so the Scrum Guide's condition for an effective Product Owner fails for at least one of them. What the role costs product teams The first cost is that accountability turns back into coordination. Evolve argues that better coordination between organisational units changes how those units work together but leaves unchanged what each one answers for (Hodgson, 2026). An AI Product Owner who negotiates AI priorities with every Product Owner is a coordination mechanism carrying an accountability title. When several managers hold partial authority over what an AI-augmented team releases, contested outputs produce meetings rather than decisions, and releases wait until everyone agrees (Hodgson, 2026). The second cost is an extra handoff, added where AI makes handoffs most expensive. AI shortens the time spent on active work but leaves the waiting time at each organisational boundary unchanged, so the share of total cycle time spent waiting rises (Hodgson, 2026). Each team that adopts AI adds requests to the AI Product Owner's queue, and the wait at that boundary lengthens with every team that joins. Reinertsen (2009) identified unmeasured queues of this kind as the main cause of long cycle times in product development, and a checkpoint with no accountability adds queue length without adding anything to the Increment (Hodgson & West, 2026). items.origTitle: O Dojo de Product Ownership: Gestão Avançada de Produtos na Era da Inteligência Artificial
items.origSummary: A maioria das organizações ainda encara a gestão de produtos como uma linha de montagem: escrever histórias de usuário, alimentar o backlog, acompanhar a velocidade das sprints e torcer para que a funcionalidade entregue gere algum resultado. Essa postura é o teto de vidro do "PO secretário de backlog". No mercado corporativo atual — pressionado por eficiência, corte de desperdício e impacto financeiro —, essa abordagem tornou-se obsoleta. Para construir produtos sustentáveis e liderar negócios com autoridade, o profissional de produto precisa trilhar a disciplina de um verdadeiro Dojo de Product Ownership . Conforme a graduação avança — da Faixa Verde à Faixa Marrom e, finalmente, à Faixa Preta —, a mentalidade muda radicalmente: sai a obsessão pelo volume de entregas e entra o domínio do discovery ágil, da saúde econômica e da estratégia de mercado. E, na nova fronteira competitiva, cada um desses graus de maturidade é impulsionado por um copiloto de Inteligência Artificial. Image 1. Faixa Verde: O Domínio do Discovery e da Validação Rápida O Faixa Verde é o profissional que rompeu definitivamente com a fábrica de entregas cegas ( build trap ). Ele não aceita pedidos de stakeholders sem questionar o problema de fundo e sabe que construir a coisa errada rapidamente continua sendo um desperdício. Foco no Problema e em Hipóteses: Em vez de pular direto para a solução, mapeia dores reais dos clientes, desenha árvores de oportunidades e estrutura experimentos enxutos para validar premissas críticas antes de acionar a engenharia. Redução de Risco de Usabilidade e Valor: Trabalha integrado ao time de design e pesquisa para garantir que o produto seja usável, viável e genuinamente desejado. O Apoio da IA no Nível Verde (O Robô de Discovery): O Faixa Verde utiliza agentes autônomos para processar centenas de entrevistas, tickets de suporte e feedbacks de usuários em minutos. A IA atua como um assistente incansável que sintetiza padrões, gera rascunhos de hipóteses ( problem statements ) e auxilia na criação rápida de especificações funcionais, liberando o PO para focar na escuta ativa e na interação humana com os clientes. Image 2. Faixa Marrom: O Domínio do Valor Econômico e da Eficiência Validar hipóteses e entregar soluções com boa usabilidade não basta se o produto queima caixa sem gerar retorno sobre o capital investido. O Faixa Marrom assume a responsabilidade pela saúde financeira da iniciativa, conectando o backlog diretamente à demonstração de resultados ( P&L ). P&L, Margens e Estratégia de Precificação: O PO domina a composição de custos diretos ( COGS ), margem bruta e lucratividade operacional. Ele compreende como cada funcionalidade ou modelo de precificação ( pricing ) afeta o fluxo de caixa e a margem de contribuição do negócio. Evidence-Based Management (EBM): Adota as quatro Áreas-Chave de Valor ( Key Value Areas ) recomendadas pela Scrum.org: Current Value (CV): O valor que o produto gera hoje em receita, retenção e satisfação. Unrealized Value (UV): A oportunidade e a fatia de mercado ainda não capturadas. Time-to-Market (T2M): A velocidade do ciclo entre formular uma hipótese, colocá-la em produção e coletar dados reais de mercado. Ability to Innovate (A2I): A capacidade do time de inovar sem ser asfixiado por débito técnico ou processos burocráticos. Cost of Delay & Matriz de ROI: Toma decisões de priorização pautadas pelo Custo do Atraso ( Cost of Delay ), garantindo que a capacidade produtiva seja alocada onde o retorno ajustado pelo risco financeiro for maior. O Apoio da IA no Nível Marrom (Dashboards Preditivos e Analytics): O Faixa Marrom opera com modelos de IA preditiva que simulam o impacto de variações de preço, projetam o P&L em tempo real e detectam anomalias nas métricas de EBM antes que elas contaminem o balanço do trimestre. 3. Faixa Preta: A Visão do Empreendedor, Três Horizontes e a Cabeça de Ponte Na Faixa Preta, o Product Owner atinge o patamar executivo descrito por Ralph Jocham e Don McGreal: o PO como um verdadeiro empreendedor e tomador de riscos corporativo. Ele equilibra a sustentação do negócio presente com a conquista de novos mercados. Gestão de Portfólio em Três Horizontes: H1 (Core): Proteção, rentabilização e eficiência da vaca leiteira atual. H2 (Escalar): Aceleração de linhas de produtos adjacentes rumo ao crescimento em escala. H3 (Futuro): Apostas disruptivas e exploração de novas fronteiras de negócio. Crossing the Chasm e a Estratégia de Cabeça de Ponte ( Beachhead Market ): Para cruzar o temido abismo entre os entusiastas ( Early Adopters ) e a maioria pragmática ( Early Majority ), o Faixa Preta recusa a armadilha de tentar vender tudo para todo mundo. Ele seleciona uma cabeça de ponte : um nicho delimitado, com uma dor financeira ou operacional tão urgente que os clientes aceitam comprar uma solução focada. Ao entregar o produto completo ( Whole Product ) e estabelecer uma reputação sólida nesse nicho, cria o efeito dominó indispensável para avançar…

items.title: The early universe wasn’t nearly as pristine as scientists thought
items.summary: JWST has revealed that galaxies were spreading carbon, oxygen, and other heavy elements through space just 500 million years after the Big Bang. The surprising discovery suggests the young universe became chemically enriched much earlier than expected, potentially erasing traces of its very first stars.

items.title: Niedrigste bisher verzeichnete Abflussmengen
items.summary: Von vielen Flüssen in Europa hat es in den vergangenen Monaten Berichte über extrem niedrige Wasserstände gegeben. Nun zeigt eine Bilanz: Europas Flüsse verzeichneten im Sommer die niedrigsten Abflussmengen seit Beginn der Aufzeichnungen im Jahr 1992.

items.summary: Die Eisschmelze in den Bergen schreitet rasant voran. Nicht zuletzt angesichts des vergangenen Sommers mit neuen Höchsttemperaturen sieht die Glaziologin Andrea Fischer Österreich auf dem Weg Richtung „Entgletscherung“.

items.title: China strebt an die Forschungsspitze
items.summary: Erstmals wurde die Tsinghua-Universität Peking im „Times Higher Education World University Ranking“ heuer vor allen kontinentaleuropäischen Universitäten eingestuft. Lange stand China in der Forschung im Schatten Europas. Doch das Kräfteverhältnis hat sich sichtlich verschoben.

items.summary: Der Organisator dieser Veranstaltung, dem Chorleiter Matthias Steiner ist es gelungen, große Sänger und Musiker für das "12. Kärntner Adventkonzert" in Stockerau zu gewinnen. items.summary: Für andere da sein, Zeit mit der Familie verbringen und Neues ausprobieren: Hermine Futschek hat auch mit 95 Jahren Freude am Leben. items.title: Studie: Leben auf Saturnmond denkbar
items.summary: Trotz eisiger Kälte und kaum Sauerstoff ist der Saturnmond Enceladus laut einer neuen Studie lebensfreundlicher als bisher angenommen. In seinem verborgenen Ozean könnten Mikroorganismen überleben.

items.title: Diese Diät kann die Alterung des Gehirns um 2,5 Jahre verlangsamen
items.summary: Menschen, die die MIND-Diät genauer befolgten, zeigten im Laufe der Zeit eine langsamere Schrumpfung des Gehirns und einen geringeren Verlust der grauen Substanz, wobei die stärksten Unterschiede einer etwa 2,5 Jahre verzögerten Gehirnalterung entsprachen. Beeren und Geflügel wurden mit gesünderen Gehirnveränderungen in Verbindung gebracht, während Süßigkeiten und frittiertes Fastfood mit einem größeren Gewebeverlust in Verbindung gebracht wurden.
items.origTitle: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.origSummary: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Schon Urzellen konnten herumkriechen
items.summary: Bereits vor rund zwei Milliarden Jahren sind die Vorläufer aller Tiere, Pflanzen und Pilze offenbar herumgekrochen: In zwanzig Minuten können Asgard-Archaeen genannte Urzellen auf diese Weise 0,06 Millimeter zurücklegen, fand ein Forschungsteam der Universität Wien nun heraus.

items.title: Vorschulkinder schaffen 18.000 Schritte
items.summary: Kleine Kinder sind deutlich bewegungsaktiver, als viele Erwachsene vermuten: Circa 18.000 Schritte am Tag sind im Alter von drei bis vier Jahren typisch. Das ergab eine internationale Studie mit mehr als 3.500 Kindern in 44 Ländern.

items.title: Könnte der Verzicht auf hochverarbeitete Lebensmittel Ihre geistige Gesundheit verbessern?
items.summary: Menschen mit Depressionen, die stark auf hochverarbeitete Lebensmittel verzichteten, erlebten in einer kleinen vorläufigen Studie bemerkenswerte Verbesserungen ihrer Symptome. Forscher vermuten, dass eine gesündere Ernährung dem Gehirn zugute kommen kann, indem sie unter anderem Darmschäden und chronische Entzündungen reduziert.
items.origTitle: Could quitting ultra-processed food boost your mental health?
items.origSummary: People with depression who dramatically cut ultra-processed foods experienced notable improvements in their symptoms in a small preliminary study. Researchers suspect healthier eating may benefit the brain partly by reducing gut damage and chronic inflammation.

items.title: Sieben und neun Jahre alte Tänzerinnen holen acht Pokale heim
items.summary: Acht Pokale für die Irish Dance Company Tulln – Nachwuchstänzerinnen holen den Sieg für Österreich TULLN/PRAG. Ein Wochenende, das für die Irish Dance Company Tulln wohl noch lange in Erinnerung bleiben wird: Bei einem internationalen Irish-Dance-Wettbewerb in Prag konnten die beiden Nachwuchstänzerinnen Leonora G. (sieben Jahre) und Paulina D. (neun Jahre) insgesamt acht Pokale nach Hause holen und damit einen besonderen Erfolg für Österreich feiern. Mit großer Freude und viel Ehrgeiz gingen...

items.title: Ein rekordverdächtiger Röntgenblitz könnte die Geburt eines Magnetars offenbaren
items.summary: Astronomen haben starke Beweise dafür gefunden, dass einige mysteriöse, minutenlange Röntgenblitze entstehen, wenn zwei Neutronensterne kollidieren und einen Magnetar erzeugen. Ein rekordverdächtiges Ereignis leuchtete fast zehn Minuten lang im Röntgenlicht und eröffnete möglicherweise einen neuen Weg, diese extremen kosmischen Verschmelzungen zu finden.
items.origTitle: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
items.origSummary: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.

items.title: Maulbeere kann Darmbakterien umgestalten und den Stoffwechsel beeinflussen
items.summary: Maulbeerverbindungen können das Darmmikrobiom auf eine Weise umgestalten, die die Darmgesundheit und den Stoffwechsel unterstützt, wobei einige Kombinationen in Tierversuchen besonders starke Wirkungen zeigten. Allerdings variieren die Ergebnisse je nach Pflanzenteil und Verarbeitungsmethode, und die Vorteile beim Menschen müssen noch bestätigt werden.
items.origTitle: Mulberry may reshape gut bacteria and influence metabolism
items.origSummary: Mulberry compounds may reshape the gut microbiome in ways that support intestinal health and metabolism, with some combinations showing especially strong effects in animal studies. However, the results vary depending on the plant part and processing method, and the benefits have yet to be confirmed in humans.

items.title: Der Marsrover Perseverance der NASA findet Grundwasser, Seen und heiße Flüssigkeiten an einem Ort
items.summary: Der Perseverance-Rover der NASA hat eine überraschend komplizierte Geschichte des Wassers im Jezero-Krater aufgedeckt. Wissenschaftler gingen davon aus, dass die Randeinheit des Kraters Seesedimente enthalten würde, fanden jedoch stattdessen uraltes magmatisches Gestein, das bei mindestens drei verschiedenen Gelegenheiten durch Wasser verändert wurde.
items.origTitle: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
items.origSummary: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.

items.title: Jets von Schwarzen Löchern könnten über das Schicksal ganzer Galaxien entscheiden
items.summary: Mächtige Jets von supermassiven Schwarzen Löchern können sternbildendes Gas weit über den sichtbaren Rand einer Galaxie hinaus stören und eine leuchtende Spur hinterlassen, die Hunderttausende Lichtjahre lang ist. Indem sie dieses Gas heiß halten und verhindern, dass es nach innen fällt, können die Jets dabei helfen, festzustellen, ob in einer Galaxie weiterhin Sterne entstehen oder ob sie still wird.
items.origTitle: Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
items.origSummary: Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.
